item.title: Embodied physical learning: a trained bacterial cell wall can guide organism behavior
item.description: arXiv:2611.07112v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Physical learning studies how physical systems themselves can be trained to perform learning tasks using physical laws. For instance, disordered spring networks can be trained by local rules to route a mechanical signal from one site in the network to another. Disordered spring networks play key roles in many facets of cell biology, not just in terms of mechanics, but also in terms of motility. How then can training on the substrate itself impact the action of an organism, such as a bacterium? Here, we train a spring-network model of the bacterial cell wall and embed it in a motile agent. The stimulus is the load the cell generates by colliding with a surface. The trained wall routes that load across the body to distant flagellar motors, where it drives stator release, and the resulting turn biases the cell toward escape and delays subsequent surface contacts. On the first near-wall tumble after entrapment, the trained cell recovers 89% of the advantage an ideal side-resolved controller provides. We call this arrangement embodied physical learning: the stimulus, the actuator, and the consequences all belong to the agent, and the training force scale is inherited from the agent's own sensing rather than imposed. An actuator with its own kinetics imposes a second, tighter constraint: the routed signal must switch the actuator within the stimulus window. We also find that behavior converges within a few hundred wall encounters, comparable to what a cell in sustained contact with structure experiences in a single generation, and that the routing survives continuous crosslink remodeling provided crucial, tension-bearing bonds are protected. Experimental tests of embodied physical learning are discussed.
item.dc:creator: Nada Elmeligy, No Chen, J. M. Schwarz

item.title: Bearing, heading and the perceptual geometry of collective motion
item.description: arXiv:2611.07214v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Traditional models of collective motion commonly assume that animals turn to match their neighbours' directions of travel. In the harmonic theory, decisions follow from a neural representation of direction, and a neighbour enters only as a stimulus at a bearing, the direction in which it lies. Here we show that a neighbour's spatial extent allows its orientation to enter through projection geometry alone, and the theory generates a matrix of coupling coefficients indexed by the neighbour's bearing and aspect. Responses to bearing alone form one edge of this matrix, and classical heading matching is a special case on its diagonal, one ray through a two-parameter family. Independently, an animal that responds only to neighbour position, perceived with a delay, acquires an alignment coefficient set by the slope of its distance-weighted attraction profile, so that it can align, anti-align or reverse sign. Alignment need not be a rule to be measured. In schooling fish and walking pigeons with body orientation measured independently of travel, social responses are recovered, including bearing responses in the fish. Heading excess depends on how turning is measured, appearing in the fish with forward but not centred responses and remaining unresolved in pigeons. Controls show why neither outcome identifies a direct alignment rule. In fish recordings with motion-assigned body polarity, heading-dependent structure departs from Vicsek form and fails the coefficient test for a common angular potential. Whether animals align thereby becomes a measurable question, with geometric, perceptual and behavioural origins that can be distinguished.
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Salahshour

item.title: Synchronized Hearts, Desynchronized Brains: A Nonlinear Dynamics Perspective for Function and Failure
item.description: arXiv:2611.06618v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Both the heart and the brain are built from electrically excitable cells, yet the emergent dynamics of these organs could not differ more. In the myocardium, a coherent traveling wave of action potentials ensures coordinated contraction; in the cerebral cortex, distributed, irregular spiking underlies efficient information processing and the generation of behavior. Here, we illuminate the principles that underlie the emergence of such distinct nonlinear dynamics using concepts from complex systems. We trace these principles across scales from ion channels and cellular action potential generation, through cellular coupling mechanisms and network architecture, to organ level dynamics and clinical phenotypes. Designed to support either synchronized waves or desynchronized information processing, the heart and the brain can thus be understood as operating on opposite sides of a synchronization phase transition. Crossing this transition implies pathological dynamics in both organs: Loss of synchrony in the heart produces arrhythmia; excess synchrony in the brain leads to epileptic seizures. We discuss how adaptation mechanisms, including plasticity, modulation, remodeling, and learning, maintain the appropriate level of (de)synchronization. Overall, we provide a unified excitable-system perspective, together with an educational notebook, to foster cross-disciplinary insights into cardiac and neural function and pathology.

item.title: Langmuir kinetics and totally asymmetric volume exclusion in linear chains via Fock space formalism
item.description: arXiv:2611.07053v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Driven-diffusive systems combining spatial exclusion and bulk exchange, such as the totally asymmetric simple exclusion process coupled with Langmuir kinetics (TASEP-LK), serve as foundational models for particle transport in vehicular traffic, conveyor networks, and mesoscopic flow channels. In this work, we employ an exact Doi-Peliti field-theoretic operator formulation in Fock space to evaluate steady-state observables, continuous phase landscapes, and spatial correlations in finite linear chains up to $k = 16$. By introducing a decomposition in terms of biorthonormal eigenvectors for asymmetric non-Hermitian matrices, the stationary state is calculated directly from the kernel of the quasi-Hamiltonian, completely bypassing the computationally prohibitive complexity of full matrix diagonalization and time-dependent matrix exponentiation. Across distinct rate regimes and global parametric scans, our exact discrete calculations demonstrate that finite-size stochastic fluctuations naturally smear out singular domain walls, producing smooth density profiles and continuous phase crossovers. Finite-size scaling illustrates how local profiles systematically steepen toward the sharp domain wall predicted by continuum field theory as $k \to \infty$. Furthermore, two-point correlation analysis reveals that in slow-kinetics regimes, spatial fluctuations generate strong inter-site cumulants, causing standard mean-field approximations to systematically underestimate joint occupancy probabilities by 50\%. These findings emphasize the necessity of analytical methods for modeling mesoscopic transport systems and short traffic corridors where local stochastic fluctuations and spatial correlations dominate the stationary dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Luis D. S. Silva, Arthur M. S. Carvalho, Francisco A. G. Almeida, Gerson C. Duarte-Filho

item.title: Interpretable many-body interaction laws for collective motion from few trajectories
item.description: arXiv:2611.08314v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Models of collective motion usually reduce social interactions to pairwise forces, despite empirical evidence for many-body effects. We introduce the directional atomic cluster expansion (dACE), which adapts the atomic cluster expansion (ACE) of interatomic potentials to self-propelled agents. dACE provides a systematically improvable, exactly equivariant expansion of an agent's acceleration that splits uniquely into 1-, 2-, 3-body and higher contributions, along with a self term for the agent's own past motion that is fitted so that it does not absorb the interactions. On simulated collectives in two and three dimensions with known rules, dACE recovers the interaction law body order by body order from little data, while the neural model SocialNet, the current closest competitor, needs more data, has much larger errors on many-body or chiral rules and is restricted to 2D. On real data sets of tracked zebrafish and golden shiners, the laws learned by dACE agree better between disjoint halves of the data than SocialNet's. The learned laws are interpretable, and in the shiners the 3-body term opposes the pairwise response as neighbourhoods get dense. Finally, we show that next-step prediction accuracy mostly measures self-propulsion and noise rather than the interactions, and suggest more robust combinations of error measures for interaction learning.
item.dc:creator: Timon S. Gutleb

item.title: A stochastic agent-based extension of the GSM$^2$ model for particle therapy: cell-cycle dynamics, dose-rate dependence, and fractionation effects
item.description: arXiv:2604.27630v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a stochastic agent-based extension of the Generalized Stochastic Microdosimetric Model (GSM$^2$) that links microscopic energy deposition by ionizing radiation to population-scale response. Each cell is represented as an agent whose DNA damage, cell-cycle phase, and fate evolve as a continuous-time Markov process. Particle arrivals, repair, misrepair, division, death, and migration are treated as competing stochastic events in an event-driven algorithm, enabling track-structure simulations of spheroids with up to $1.5\times10^5$ cells in minutes on a single workstation. For static populations, the model reproduces the Lea--Catcheside dose-rate dependence of survival for proton and carbon-ion irradiation over four orders of magnitude in dose rate. Dose-rate sparing decreases with increasing LET and disappears for low-energy carbon ions. After calibration to a single survival curve for aerobic X-ray irradiation of V79 spheroids, the model predicts without further fitting survival under anoxia and after carbon-ion irradiation in aerobic and anoxic conditions, reproducing measured oxygen enhancement ratios and relative biological effectiveness. Applied to three-dimensional tumor spheroids, the framework resolves responses to single, split, and fractionated irradiations, separates the effects of repair, reassortment, and repopulation, and quantifies stochastic variability between realizations. The model provides a mechanistic single-cell framework for studying time-dependent effects and uncertainty in particle irradiation.
item.dc:creator: Francesco G. Cordoni, Marco Battestini, Marta Missiaggia

item.title: Metastable phase separation and information retrieval in multicomponent mixtures
item.description: arXiv:2509.10705v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Liquid mixtures can separate into phases with distinct composition. This phenomenon has recently come back to prominence due to its role in complex biological liquids, such as the cytoplasm, which contain thousands of components. For simple two-component mixtures phase-separated states are global free energy minima. However, local free energy minima, i.e., metastable states, are known to play a dominant role in complex systems with many components. For example, Hopfield neural networks can retrieve stored information from partial cues via relaxation to metastable states. Under what conditions can phase separated states be metastable, and what are the implications for information retrieval in multicomponent liquids? In this work we develop the general thermodynamic formalism of metastable phase separation. We then apply this formalism to an illustrative toy example inspired by recent experiments, binary mixtures with high-order interactions. Finally, as core application of the formalism, we study metastability in Hopfield liquids, a class of multicomponent mixtures capable of storing information on the composition of phases. We show that these phases can be nucleated from partial cues via metastable phase separation. Spatial simulations of liquids with a large number of components match our analytical solution. Our work suggests that complex biological mixtures can retrieve information through metastable phase separation.
item.dc:creator: Davide Marcato, Rodrigo Braz Teixeira, Izaak Neri, Pablo Sartori

item.title: Controlling microalgae populations by phototactic memory
item.description: arXiv:2601.07741v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Motile microorganisms navigate environments that vary in space and time by coupling sensory inputs to internal physiological states and active motion. In photosynthetic microorganisms, such coupling can be mediated by phototaxis, yet how temporal sensing combines with spatial variations of the environment to shape population organisation remains poorly understood. To probe this coupling, we expose populations of the phototactic microalga \textit{Chlamydomonas reinhardtii} to structured light landscapes. Under ring-shaped illumination, cells robustly accumulate at the center of the illuminated region, rather than at the light-intensity maximum. Single-cell tracking shows that cells steer relative to local intensity gradients and undergo a non-trivial phototactic response, where, on average, cells outside the ring perform positive phototaxis while cells inside perform negative phototaxis. Population experiments, numerical simulations and analytical modelling show that this trapping cannot be reproduced by an instantaneous switching rule, but requires a finite phototactic memory acting on the transition between positive and negative phototaxis. This internal timescale couples to the geometry of the light field and to the persistence of active motion, enabling controllable spatial localisation without physical confinement. Our results generically show how memory in a single-cell sensory response can control population-level organisation in a living active system.
item.dc:creator: Gianni Jacucci, Davide Breoni, Pierre Illien, Luca Tubiana, Jean-Fran\c{c}ois Allemand, Sylvain Gigan, Rapha\"el Jeanneret

item.title: Inclined surfaces bias bacterial swarming expansion and edge organization
item.description: arXiv:2610.01281v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Bacterial swarming is the collective expansion of dense populations of motile cells across hydrated soft surfaces, yet gravity is usually treated as a fixed background condition in standard horizontal assays. We used surface inclination to examine how agar-surface orientation relative to gravity affects the expansion of Enterobacter sp. SM3 swarms. At macroscopic scales, we found that colony expansion depended non-monotonically on inclination, with the strongest spreading at intermediate inclinations and weaker expansion under shallow or near-inverted conditions. Paired up-facing acute and down-facing obtuse configurations with the same tilt magnitude showed different expansion responses, suggesting that swarm expansion depended on both tilt magnitude and which side of the agar surface faced upward relative to gravity. Inclination also produced downhill-biased colony morphologies. For microscopic scales, particle image velocimetry (PIV) analysis showed generally lower mean activity under inclination than in the flat references, with a non-monotonic angular response. The downhill tip showed slower motion, shorter spatial correlations and smaller vortex cores than the upper region. To interpret the macroscopic trends, we extended a two-phase thin-film model by introducing an effective gravity coupling projected normal and tangential to the agar surface. Simulations suggest that the surface-tangential component mainly drives lateral redistribution, whereas the surface-normal component modifies film pressure and helps distinguish up-facing from down-facing configurations.
item.dc:creator: Pengxi Gu, Zixiang Lin, Hui Ren, Jin Zhu, Anqi Li, Omar Said, Weijie Chen, Zijie Qu
